AI Weekly Digest
October 26, 2026
A few things worth knowing this week — here's what's happening in AI, in plain English.
TL;DR — Top picks this week
AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says
An economist at Apollo says that despite all the money companies are pouring into AI and all the hype, it hasn't produced any actual financial gains for companies outside the tech industry. For us, this is a reminder to be cautious about AI spending and to expect clear, measurable business results from any AI projects we take on.
Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
Pennsylvania has passed a new law requiring that any ad created or significantly changed by AI — whether an image, video, audio, or text — must carry a label disclosing that. If we run or create advertising in Pennsylvania, we may need to add AI disclosures to our ads to stay compliant.
Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
Google has changed its privacy policy so that personal data from Gmail, Google Photos, and Drive could be used to show you targeted ads if you use Google's personalized AI features. If any of us use these Google AI features, our personal files and emails may factor into the ads we see, which is worth knowing from both a privacy and a marketing perspective.
🛠️ Tools & Products
Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
This article is a roundup of AI assistants that can operate directly inside text messages, covering everything from general helpers to ones built for families, travel, and work. It matters to us because it shows how AI is becoming easier to access through everyday tools like texting, which could change how our teams and customers get assistance.
Read more →
Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
OpenAI upgraded its online storage system, called Habitat, by using shared resources, worldwide caching, and a cloud database, which makes data reads about 12 times faster for ChatGPT. This faster access helps keep the service responsive and able to support a huge number of users, which could improve the reliability of any AI tools we rely on.
Read more →
🏢 Industry & Adoption
AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says
An economist at Apollo says that despite all the money companies are pouring into AI and all the hype, it hasn't produced any actual financial gains for companies outside the tech industry. For us, this is a reminder to be cautious about AI spending and to expect clear, measurable business results from any AI projects we take on.
Read more →
The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
This article keeps a running list of AI projects that shut down or fell short of expectations, including Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI and OpenAI's rocky launch of a 'super app' (an all-in-one app combining many services). It's a useful reminder that even the biggest companies struggle to deliver on AI, so we should temper expectations when evaluating AI tools and vendors.
Read more →
The new economics of enterprise AI
This article argues that AI is becoming like electricity for companies: at first, only a few uses exist and cost isn't a concern, but once it underpins everything, efficiency becomes the key question. For us, that means as AI tools spread across our work, we'll eventually be judged not just on whether we use AI, but on how efficiently and cost-effectively we use it.
Read more →
AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
This piece looks at how AI adoption is spreading across industries, arguing that tech is just the first sector to be affected and other industries are next. It matters to us because the changes now happening in tech roles could soon reshape work in our own industry, including areas like sales, operations, and finance.
Read more →
🔬 Research
Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
A new study found that when asked to pick between candidates, the AI chatbot Grok favored Republicans while OpenAI's GPT favored Democrats, and the two disagreed in more than 90% of nearly 500 election races. This matters to us because it shows AI tools can carry built-in biases, so we should be cautious about relying on AI recommendations without checking them.
Read more →
Making the case for context-aware AI
This article makes the case that AI tools need to understand how a business actually operates, because even powerful AI can miss the real-world constraints and relationships that make a decision right or wrong. It matters to us because if we want AI to help with daily operations rather than just experiments, it needs to be connected to our company's actual way of working.
Read more →
🛡️ Safety & Policy
Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
Pennsylvania has passed a new law requiring that any ad created or significantly changed by AI — whether an image, video, audio, or text — must carry a label disclosing that. If we run or create advertising in Pennsylvania, we may need to add AI disclosures to our ads to stay compliant.
Read more →
Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
Google has changed its privacy policy so that personal data from Gmail, Google Photos, and Drive could be used to show you targeted ads if you use Google's personalized AI features. If any of us use these Google AI features, our personal files and emails may factor into the ads we see, which is worth knowing from both a privacy and a marketing perspective.
Read more →
OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
OpenAI has announced it will stop letting its most advanced AI models learn from the live internet, saying doing so carries significant risks. This could affect how quickly AI tools improve and change over time, which matters if we rely on AI products in our work.
Read more →
Securing our frontier model training environment
OpenAI added stronger safety measures around training its most advanced models, including keeping the work in isolated offline environments and running intensive tests to spot problems. These protections lower the chance of accidental leaks or misuse, giving us more confidence in the safety of AI technologies we might adopt.
Read more →
